title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer inceleme: Arcade yarış oyunlarına hızlı dönüş
summary: Fuse Games tarafından geliştirilen Star Wars: Galactic Racer, roguelike unsurları ve yüksek hızıyla arcade yarış türüne soluk getiriyor.
body:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer, VGC, Polygon, Kotaku ve The Verge gibi teknoloji ve oyun yayınlarının incelemelerine göre oyunculara yüksek hızlı bir arcade yarış deneyimi sunuyor. İmparatorluğun düşüşünden sonra geçen yapımda oyuncular, gezegenler arası yarışlarda mücadele eden Shade adlı gizemli bir pilotu yönetiyor.

## Roguelike mekanikler ve yüksek hız

Fuse Games imzasını taşıyan yapım, klasik arcade yarış türünü roguelike yapısıyla birleştiriyor. Kotaku'nun aktardığına göre, her oturumda sunulan lig giriş belirteci başarısız olunması durumunda kaybediliyor ve oyuncuların seriye baştan başlaması gerekiyor. Bu durum yarışlara yüksek bir risk unsuru katarken, Polygon'a göre oyuncuların araç geliştirme ve yetenek yönetimi gibi stratejik kararlar almasını da zorunlu kılıyor.

## Araç çeşitliliği ve platformlar

Oyuncular landspeeder, speeder bike, skim speeder ve ikonik podracer olmak üzere farklı sürüş dinamiklerine sahip araçlar arasından seçim yapabiliyor. PC, Xbox Series X/S ve PS5 Pro platformları için 6 Ekim 2026 tarihinde çıkış yapan oyun; görselleri, John Williams tarzı orkestral müzikleri ve Burnout serisini hatırlatan rakip eleme mekanikleriyle dikkat çekiyor.

**Neden önemli?** Uzun süredir yeni bir temsilcisi çıkmayan arcade yarış türünü rogue-lite yapısıyla yeniden yorumlayan Star Wars: Galactic Racer, hem serinin hayranlarına hem de türün meraklılarına yenilikçi bir oynanış sunuyor.

source_texts.title: Star Wars Galactic Racer review: Somehow, Burnout returns in a modern racing classic
source_texts.summary: The thrilling throwback to arcade racing's glory days wows with visual might and a great single-player offering
source_texts.text:
We really didn’t know how good we had it when you’d get 10 different racing games every Christmas. The variety, inventiveness, and sheer volume of different racing experiences were once a hallmark of the yearly gaming lineup, but that’s now all but disappeared.
As Burnout, Need for Speed, Midnight Club, Project Gotham Racing, and others fell away, virtually only Forza remains, carrying the flame for a much-loved genre. Now Star Wars: Galactic Racer is here, and it’s a throwback to the glory days of PS2 racing, and one of the best arcade racers in years.
Set in the days following the fall of the Empire, Star Wars: Galactic Racer follows Shade, a mysterious racer who sets out for revenge on the pompous Kestar Boole, a racing superstar and someone you’d love to see crash into a wall at top speed.
The game’s campaign sees Shade competing in a series of events which span across familiar Star Wars planets, before culminating in a championship race.
This is no simple campaign mode, however. The game is run-based, meaning at the start of each session, you’re given a league entry token. If you fail to meet the race objective, your league entry token is lost, and you have to start the whole racing series over again.
This gives the campaign races some real stakes. It’s not utterly brutal â you don’t have to come first absolutely every time, but you certainly have to compete if you’re going to progress the story.
After each race you’ll be given a reward based on your position which you can use to upgrade your ship. This can be a new ability, and increase in stats, or a new part which will make you stronger for the upcoming race.
The loop is essentially winning races to make your ship better, in order to win more races. If you’re on a hot streak, it’s easy to consistently rack up the wins and progress through the game’s campaign at a high clip. As you progress in the campaign, new factors like race sponsors change the way you earn credits.
For example, I was sponsored by The Hutts, which meant that for every second I spent in first place, I’d earn more credits. Other credit bonuses are earned by doing things like using abilities in a race, or taking down your competitors.
Speaking of taking down your competitors, this is where the game’s Burnout lineage is most apparent. Smash into your fellow racer hard enough and they’ll fly into the closest wall and burst into flames. The game even features the classic Burnout camera which shows your pal exploding into tiny pieces while you fly away. This is always satisfying, and adds a level of danger to the races which is amplified by the game’s incredible sense of speed.
You can respawn after you crash or are destroyed, but these are limited, so being careful about who is around you, and making liberal use of your defensive abilities is a must.
This becomes most prominent in race types like Elimination, which sees the player in last place of the race being eliminated after a set amount of time, until only the top two remain. You can be having the race of your life, but one lapse in concentration can see the whole thing fall apart, much like your speeder as it becomes close friends with the wall.
This, tied to the perilous nature of the league entry token, only heightens the stakes. During Career you’re often presented with two different race types to choose from to progress the story. One of these could be an Eliminator, while the other may be a test flight in a pod racer, which won’t end your story run even if you die. However, the rewards from the Eliminator are much higher than that of the test flight, which encourages the player to take the risk, knowing that you could substantially improve your ship.
There are three main types of vehicles â a landspeeder (think Luke’s from Episode 4), a speeder bike (think Endor chase in Episode 6) and the skim speeder, a new vehicle which is being introduced to the Star Wars canon via this game. Each ship can be massively customised from changing the entire body of the ship, to cosmetic elements like the colour and finish of each.
Each of the three has their own advantages and drawbacks, but the game does a very good job at not making them handle exactly the same. I genuinely felt like each ship was substantially different, especially when you further upgrade them through a single-player run.
Pod racing is also in the game, as are some classic pod racers from Episode 1. Pod racing also feels hugely different from standard races, primarily because it’s so much harder than the others. The speed of the pod racers is excitingly jarring, and there’s a steep learning curve compared to the ships you’ll fly in the campaign.
This sense of speed and danger is heightened by the game’s presentation, which is stellar. Sure, it’s a video game cheat code to have the Star Wars sound library and musical cues, but the way they’re used is expert.
When ships fly into caves, the roar of the engines is muted, making it feel claustrophobic. A near-horror game emerges as multiple ships aim for a narrow passage way through a mountain, only for the tension to be broken by emerging into an expansive landscape.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer also looks great, and does a very impressive job at making the tracks readable, even when you’re travelling towards them at unfathomable speeds.
I’d have loved a few more planets to explore, and this is something that will hopefully come with future DLC. It’s not as if there’s a shortage of Star Wars locales to choose from.
My only real drawback is that due to the game being set in a specific point in the Star Wars canon, there isn’t much room for silly cameos from across the series. Sebulba, Dud Bolt and Ben Quadinaros being in the game will pop the irony-poisoned millennials that grew up on the Episode 1 racer N64 and arcade games, but names and faces you’ll recognise are few and far between.
I understand not having Force Ghost Darth Vader in a tiny TIE Fighter in the single-player, but the arcade mode feels ripe to really have fun with the license in a way the game doesn’t quite do currently.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a thrilling throwback to a better time for racing games. It’s thrilling, fun, and genuinely innovative in ways that make it a game not to be missed this year.
Star Wars fans will have an amazing time, but anyone who’s even racing game-adjacent should absolutely consider it. It’s a game from an era that gave us Blur, Split/Second, and the desperately missed Burnout, and it carries on that legacy with pride.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review
Star Wars: Galactic Racer absolutely nails what it is trying to do. It is a high-octane racer that's endless fun to play, and it looks fantastic. This would have been a great game with a standard single-player mode, but what is here is inventive and engaging. I'd have loved a few silly classic characters and another planet or two, but this is a game I'll return to for a long time.
- Racing feels excellent.
- Superb presentation.
- Single-play

source_texts.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is the Best Arcade Racing Game in a Generation
source_texts.summary: The PS5, Xbox, and PC game blends roguelikes with Burnout, Wipeout, and F-Zero to brutal and brilliant effect
source_texts.text:
Racing game fans don't get a new release like Star Wars: Galactic Racer every day. We don't get one every year. Recently, we haven't even got one every console generation. We should savor it.
I'm not talking about the Star Wars licensing, even though this is the first Star Wars racing game since 2002. Although, now I mention it, we should savor that too. Galactic Racer sure makes the most of it, with its bombastic John Williams-esque orchestral soundtrack, its vivid cast of squabbling alien racers, its stark planetary biomes, and above all, the thrilling roars, flutters, and screams of its audio design. Speed never sounded so good as it does in Star Wars.
But for a certain kind of racing game fan, Galactic Racer is even more consequential than that. The genre is in desperate need of new ideas, and Galactic Racer developer Fuse Games — founded by former Criterion Games staff (Burnout, Need for Speed) — has plenty. There hasn't been a racing game this structurally innovative in a long, long time.
There hasn't been an arcade racer this good in even longer. Let me be clear about the genre distinction I'm drawing here: I consider Mario Kart and its imitators to belong to their own kart-racing subgenre, while Forza Horizon or The Crew sit at the approachable end of real-world driving games. When I talk about arcade racers, I mean games that are all about immediacy and velocity, where the brake pedal is a foreign object and where pure racing meets high-concept video-gamey mechanics, usually involving boost. Games like, well, Burnout.
Galactic Racer is more than a bit Burnout, as you'd expect, with its crashes and takedowns and focus on maintaining semi-permanent boost. As an anti-grav racer, it also takes a fair bit from F-Zero and Wipeout. Surprisingly, it might take more from the former, in its focus on sheer, blinding pace over a heavier sense of inertia. It's not that it doesn't have physics, it's that its racing craft are too fast for the laws of physics to properly register.
Galactic Racer is hard, innovative, and there's a lot going on
Yes, this is a purebred arcade racer. But it's also a roguelike (or a roguelite, to be exact). This is where things get really interesting. Galactic Racer has a run-based campaign structure that sees you undertake branching Tours of randomized events. Wrecking your craft with multiple crashes — or failing to make the top three in an Eliminator race, say — can send you all the way back to the start of a new Tour.
This game is also a quasi-RPG, where stat boosts, status effects, and buildcrafting all play a huge part. There's a wide range of playstyles you can assemble from its component parts. At the start of a run, you choose from three vehicle types, 14 racing styles with different traits and starting abilities, and game-modifying Favors. During a run, you earn new upgrades, abilities, and parts for your craft that enhance its abilities in specific conditions.
Those conditions add another vector to this complex web. Planetary conditions make a big difference to things like cornering and engine cooling; some courses thread through acid rivers that can disable your electrics if you're unshielded. Much of the game revolves around optimizing how you cycle between two boost mechanics, the safe Afterburner and the more dramatic Ramjet, which can blow you up if it overheats. A build focused on Ramjet cooling, allowing you to maintain its boost indefinitely, can be really powerful. But you might want to concentrate on shields, or offensive takedown abilities, or other areas instead.
As you can see, there's an awful lot going on here, both in the meta of a run and in the moment-to-moment of Galactic Racer's very fast-paced events. The game has little in the way of tutorials, which I think might be a mistake; you can be deep into it before you fully understand how you acquire certain status effects, what they do, and how best to exploit or negate them. It's the way of the roguelike to encourage players to discover its mysteries over the long haul, but this is an unfamiliar setting for that kind of game design, and it will leave many players struggling to catch up.
It's also a hard game. I'm a seasoned, if not highly skilled, player of racing games, and I found it a shock to the system. Crashing out of a run several events in, just because you hit the wall too many times on an unfamiliar track, feels brutal. The art style is evocative and very Star Wars, but its naturalism isn't overloaded with visual cues, and tracks can be hard to read at speed. The game's learning curve is steep, and there's a lot to manage and think about in a race.
But boy, when you get there, the rush is unmatched. This is a game of both blistering speed and tactical nuance, where smart use of your abilities is just as important as racing reflexes. It's a deep game system, and the further you get into a run, the better and more rewarding it gets.
Campaign is king, but multiplayer is a brilliant surprise
Galactic Racer's campaign mode is clearly what the game has been designed around, and it's a show-stopper. You play as Shade, a freelance pilot entering the Galactic Racing League and challenging an aristocratic champion whose family enslaves your people. Without going too heavy on story — which is usually a mistake in a racing game — the campaign offers lots of enjoyable Star Wars color and some memorable characters, including the stout, mustachioed alien who runs the racing league and acts as your avuncular backer. More to the point, the full roguelite structure gives the game's systems the room they need to breathe.
The other single-player modes are simpler. Scenarios are truncated, five-race tours starring some of the other racers, and worth doing just to fully understand some of the playstyle and build options. The Arcade is mostly time trials, and is the first (but not only) place you will encounter podracing, the inhumanly fast discipline featured in The Phantom Menace. (Yes, podracer supreme Sebulba is in the game, too.)
The pleasant surprise of the package is multiplayer, specifically Multiplayer Tour. This mode effectively condenses a campaign run into five races, with a build phase, during which you earn upgrades, parts, and abilities and slap an effective build together as best you can, capped off with a championship race that decides the result. It's spiced up by a betting system where you can reap extra rewards by predicting your own finishing places, and who will win overall. It's a brilliant, fresh take on online racing that is sure to find its fans, if Fuse Games can balance it in the wild.
Star Wars fans with fond memories of Episode 1: Racer will love Galactic Racer's rich fan-service and handsome production values, but they might find its complexity and difficulty to be a rude — and initially confusing — awakening. source_texts.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer: The Kotaku Review
source_texts.summary: Ain’t no lightsabers or Skywalkers in this new Star Wars game, which is great
source_texts.text:
The podracing sequence in 1999’s Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace is probably the one part of the Star Wars prequels most people, even non-fans, can agree is really cool. Weird aliens zipping around at impossible speeds in clunky machines that make strange noises that seem one bump away from falling apart.Â
And Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a video game dedicated entirely to recreating and expanding on that one genuinely awesome bit from the prequels. Like any good podracer or speeder bike, it has some imperfections. Some dents. But none of these issues hold back Galactic Racer from crossing the finish line and becoming one of my favorite Star Wars games in years.Â
Welcome to the Galactic League!
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is set sometime after the events of Return of the Jedi, likely around the time of The Force Awakens, but before the First Order shows up and starts causing chaos. The thing is, Galactic Racer isnât really concerned about being part of a larger Star Wars story or connecting dots between moments in the canon. And thatâs great! Not every Star Wars game needs to be concerned with Luke Skywalker or the Rebels or whatever.Â
Instead, you play as a new character, Shade, who, through some trickery, ends up in a large galactic racing league with the goal of beating the reigning champ. That champion is Kestar Bool, a smug bastard who is part of a powerful and rich alien family that brutally invaded and took control of Shadeâs planet years ago. So Shade is eager to beat him and help kick him out of the league before he can take it over.Â
To beat Kestar Bool, Shade will have to do a lot of galactic racing. And this is where Galactic Racer really shines, as no matter what youâre driving, the game feels very fast and runs perfectly.
It didnât matter if I hopped into a speeder bike, landspeeder, skimmer, or even a podracer; all of them whipped around the gameâs various race tracks at screaming speeds. Cutting through a cave or trying to take a small shortcut at these speeds is genuinely difficult, and it doesnât take much to crash and burn. I think I stopped blinking for extended periods of time while racing around planets like Tatooine and Ando Prime.Â
Each of the different kinds of space-racing vehicles in Galactic Racer feels totally different to pilot, too.Â
Landspeeders love to drift, but take time to reach top speed. Meanwhile, skimmers use their movable fins to turn tightly and never slow down. Speeder bikes offer bursts of incredible speed and acceleration, but offer little protection against aggressive racers trying to bash you off the track. And then you have podracers, which move faster than anything else in the game and feel like theyâre about to explode if you look at them the wrong way. I really enjoyed learning how to master each type of vehicle, even if I ended up preferring the landspeeder over the rest.Â
The other thing youâll have to master is how boosting works in Galactic Racer. You have a basic âturboâ button that uses up a meter. But thereâs also your âRamjet,â a sort of super-boost that you can activate thatâs even faster, but if not used correctly, will literally blow up your vehicle. Though you can still win a race if you cross the line as you blow up. Trust me.
Managing these two boosts while drifting around tracks and dodging hazards such as acid and lava, and also managing different abilities like shields, can be a lot.Â
Early on, I slammed into a lot of rocks and lost a lot of races. However, as I learned how to handle the speed and the controls, I fell in love with the smooth racing on offer in Galactic Racer. It just feels so damn good to drive around in this game. Even better when I got to slam another racer into a wall and got a slow-mo view of them eating it.Â
Flipping switches and winning races
The gameâs main campaign mode, starring Shade taking on Kestar Bool, is built around a roguelike progression system where you start a season with a crappy new vehicle and then upgrade and improve it as you win races across multiple planets.Â
If you crash a few too many times or lose a few key races during a season, youâll have to restart with a new vehicle and make your way through a new selection of randomly picked events and races.Â
This setup makes each race in Galactic Racer much more intense. Every crash builds towards a failure. Even just smashing into walls or other racers too much at high speed can break parts of your vehicle and add negative status effects, like making your speeder drift in one direction.Â
When these parts break, thereâs a small QTE mini-game you can play to try to avoid picking up a negative effect. And nailing those QTEs made me feel like Anakin Skywalker flipping switches in his podracer to make it work again. Mess those up, though, and it can be a big problem, especially if you donât have the resources to fix these malfunctions; it can make a season much trickier to win.Â
I loved building up a racing vehicle with upgrades and new parts, adding shields or boosters to make it tougher or faster. There are a ton of parts and upgrades to unlock via winning. And you eventually get the ability to pick a sponsor, like a racing-loving Hutt gangster, who offers even more upgrades and resources if you keep winning and completing other challenges on the track. Fail too much, however, and your benefactor will ditch you.Â
The racing is even more exciting in this mode as you can develop rivalries with the other NPC racers, some of whom are real assholes. Eventually, this can lead to one-on-one challenge races against your rivals to prove who really is the best. Play your cards right, though, and by the end of the story, you might be able to win over some of these bastards to help you take down Kestar Bool.Â

-                  Disliked On-foot segments are lackluster.

Off the track, Galactic Racerâs main mode does suffer from some stale on-foot sequences that donât add much and quickly start to feel repetitive. Then again, during these segments you get to chat up Sebulba and even experience past podraces he won back in the day, so it’s not all bad. I just wish these on-foot areas felt more varied as you visited other planets and werenât filled with the same conversations and animations.Â
